t: The Genealogy and Birth of Jesus
set: Judea under Roman rule, with Herod the Great as client king. Lineage mattered enormously here — for property, priesthood, and above all for any claim to be the promised Messiah, who Scripture said would come from David's line.

his.t: Herod the Great rules as Rome's client king and has no claim to David's throne.
Rome ruled the land, and many Jews hoped for a son of David to restore their kingdom.

cus.t: Betrothal was legally binding, so ending it took a formal divorce.
Jewish family lists usually named fathers only, so Matthew's four women stand out.

cu: Betrothal was legally binding in first-century Judea — breaking it required a formal divorce, which is why Joseph's plan to end things "quietly" (v.19) was an act of mercy, not a small gesture.

ot.n: God's covenant promise to David of an everlasting throne — the promise this genealogy is built to fulfill.
The virgin-birth prophecy Matthew quotes directly in v.23.
God's promise to Abraham that all nations would be blessed through his offspring.

im.c: The Nativity, by Gustave Doré (1866)

cm.n: Clarke draws attention to the four women named in the genealogy — Tamar and Bathsheba, both involved in scandal, and Rahab and Ruth, both Gentiles with no natural claim to Israel's covenant. He reads their inclusion as a deliberate signal, planted right at the Gospel's opening, that Christ came to save sinners and that God's salvation was never intended for Jews alone.
Henry argues this genealogy is neither pointless nor a vanity project — it functions as legal evidence, proving Jesus's right to be recognized as the promised descendant of both Abraham and David.

JFB notes that "the book of the generation" is a distinctly Jewish phrase (it echoes Genesis 5:1), functioning as a title for just this genealogy section rather than the whole Gospel. They stress this is specifically Joseph's lineage — and although Joseph wasn't Jesus's biological father, his own well-established descent from David was exactly what secured Jesus's legal claim…

Lewis does not comment on Matthew 1, but in Miracles his chapter "The Grand Miracle" treats the Incarnation as the central miracle of Christianity, with the others either preparing for it or following from it. He pictures it as a great descent, like a diver who goes down to the bottom of the sea and rises again with the lost things in his hands.

set: Herod the Great rules Judea as a Roman client king (37-4 BC) — a brilliant builder and ruthless ruler known for killing rivals, including his own family. Bethlehem sits about six miles south of Jerusalem; Galilee, where the family eventually settles, was viewed by Judeans as rustic backcountry.

his.t: Herod ruled 37 to 4 BC, built grand projects, and killed rivals, even his own sons.
Visitors from the East stirred fears, since Parthia had invaded Judea decades earlier.

cus.t: Magi were scholar-priests who studied stars and dreams, likely from Persia.
Gold, frankincense and myrrh were costly gifts, fit for a king.

cu: The Magi were likely scholar-astrologers from Persia, a class that studied stars and dreams for signs — their gifts of gold, frankincense, and myrrh were fitting tribute for a king.

ot.n: The prophecy of Bethlehem as the Messiah's birthplace, quoted directly by the chief priests in v.6.
"Out of Egypt I called My Son" — originally about Israel's exodus, applied by Matthew to Jesus.
Rachel weeping for her children — the lament Matthew connects to Herod's massacre.

im.c: The Magi Journeying, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Barnes takes a notably historical, less speculative approach than his contemporaries — he identifies the Magi as respected Persian or Arabian court philosophers and astronomers, not sorcerers, and treats their star as most likely a low-altitude luminous phenomenon rather than a literal star, since actual stars are far too vast and distant to guide travelers on a road.

Henry paints Herod's scheme in vivid terms: thinking he had "burnt the hive" by killing the infants of Bethlehem, Herod imagined he had also "killed the master bee" — but God only laughs at such plots from heaven.

JFB notes Herod's questioning of the wise men was calculated and secretive — he needed the star's exact timing to estimate the child's age, and didn't want his intentions suspected. When his plan ultimately failed, JFB observes that Herod wasn't outwitted by the wise men at all, but by God Himself, who "disappointeth the devices of the crafty."

t: The Mission of John the Baptist
set: About AD 26-29, under Roman rule. Israel had gone centuries without a widely recognized prophet — John's sudden appearance breaks that long silence, deliberately echoing Elijah in both message and appearance.

his.t: Pharisees and Sadducees held religious power under Rome, and John's warning aimed at them.
Rome ruled Judea through a governor, and Herod's son Antipas ruled Galilee.

cus.t: John's camel-hair clothes and leather belt matched Elijah's, a deliberate prophetic sign.
Locusts were a clean food under the Law and a common desert meal.

cu: John's camel-hair garment and leather belt mirror Elijah's description in 2 Kings 1:8. Ritual washing existed in Judaism already, but John's baptism was distinct — it required personal repentance and pointed forward to the Messiah.

ot.n: "A voice crying in the wilderness" — quoted directly as describing John's role.
The promised messenger who prepares the way before the Lord.
"You are My Son" — echoed in the Father's declaration at the baptism.

im.c: John the Baptist Baptizes Jesus, by Gustave Doré

cm.n: Drawing on rabbinic writings, Gill notes that Jewish tradition itself directly tied repentance to the Messiah's arrival — one saying held that Israel would remain unredeemed without national repentance, but that even a single day of it could bring the Messiah at once.

Henry poetically frames John as "the morning star" whose rising gives way to Christ, "the Sun of righteousness." He notes that Jesus submitted to baptism despite having no sin of His own to confess — deliberately modeling the pattern of doing first and teaching second, which Henry says every minister of the gospel ought to follow after Him.

JFB points out that "the kingdom of heaven is at hand" is a phrase found in none of the other Gospels, yet appears nearly thirty times in Matthew alone — a mark of this Gospel's distinctly Jewish framing. On "brood of vipers," they read it as a charge that the Pharisees and Sadducees, despite their mutual rivalry, were united in poisoning the nation's true spiritual life.

set: The rugged Judean desert west of the Dead Sea, then a deliberate move north to Capernaum — a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee sitting on the Via Maris, a major trade highway linking Egypt and Damascus.

his.t: It had many Gentiles and was seen by Judeans as rural backcountry.
Fishing was a family business, so leaving boats and nets meant leaving income.

cus.t: Flat round loaves were the daily staple, so turning stones to bread meant ending hunger.
Fishermen cast round nets by hand, then mended them on the shore.

cu: Forty days of fasting deliberately parallels Israel's forty years in the wilderness and Moses' forty-day fast on Sinai — where Israel failed repeatedly, Jesus stands firm.

ot.n: "Man does not live on bread alone" — Jesus' first response to the devil, quoted directly.
"Do not put the Lord your God to the test" — Jesus' second response.
The prophecy of light dawning on Galilee, quoted as fulfilled in v.15-16.

im.c: The Temptation of Christ, by Ary Scheffer (1854)

cm.n: Wesley connects Jesus' forty days in the wilderness directly to two towering Old Testament precedents: Moses, who fasted forty days as the giver of the Law, and Elijah, who did the same as its great restorer.

Henry observes that temptation directly follows Jesus' greatest moment of divine affirmation at His baptism — a pattern he sees throughout Scripture, where great privilege and special favor never exempt anyone from being tested. He draws a deliberate parallel between Satan's triumph over the first Adam in Eden and his ultimate defeat here by Christ, the second Adam.

JFB carefully notes how Matthew's account of calling Peter and Andrew differs from John's Gospel — in John, Andrew first seeks out Jesus while still in Judea; here, Jesus Himself directly calls the two brothers by the Sea of Galilee, after returning north following John's arrest. They treat these as two distinct moments, not a contradiction.

set: Traditionally located near the "Horns of Hattin" overlooking the Sea of Galilee — a natural amphitheater where a seated teacher's voice could carry to a large crowd. Jewish religious life at the time centered on synagogue teaching and Pharisaic tradition, the very target of much of this sermon.

his.t: Heavy taxes and Roman rule left many poor, so the Beatitudes spoke to real need.
Soldiers could force civilians to carry loads, behind "go the second mile."

cus.t: A rabbi sat to teach with authority, so Jesus visibly takes that role.
Salt flavored and preserved food and was valuable, so salt that lost its taste was useless.

cu: Sitting down to teach (v.1) was the customary posture of a rabbi with authority — Jesus visibly takes that role. The everyday images throughout (salt, oil lamps, city walls) would have been immediately familiar to His audience.

ot.n: A similar "blessed is the one who..." structure opens the entire Psalter.
The Law passages Jesus repeatedly cites and deepens throughout the "You have heard... but I tell you" section.
"The meek shall inherit the land" — the background for the Beatitude in v.5.

im.c: The Sermon on the Mount, by Gustave Doré (1866)

cm.n: Henry makes a striking observation: classical philosophers never counted humility among the virtues, yet Christ places poverty of spirit first, before every other beatitude. He reads it as the necessary foundation for all the rest — "those who would build high must begin low" — self-emptying as the soil in which every other grace can take root.

On "salt of the earth," JFB notes real scholarly disagreement over whether salt can even chemically lose its saltiness — but argues the point of Jesus' image doesn't depend on resolving that question. What matters is the implication: if the very thing meant to preserve the world's moral health loses its own distinct character, nothing else is left to do that job.

Clarke traces "mercy" to its Latin root — miserans (pitying) joined with cor (heart) — literally "pain of heart" felt on another's behalf. He also grounds "a city set on a hill" in real geography, citing a 17th-century traveler's account of the actual rise near the Sea of Galilee traditionally identified as the site of this sermon.

Lewis does not comment on Matthew 5 verse by verse, but his chapter "Counting the Cost" in Mere Christianity takes up verse 48, "Be perfect." He says we should expect more than a patch-up job: God means to make us what He says, like a man who thinks he is having a few leaks fixed and finds that the owner is building a palace on the spot.

t: Prayer, Fasting, and Trust in God
set: First-century Judean society prized public honor. Acts of charity were sometimes announced with a trumpet-like signal at festivals, and prominent giving chests sat in synagogues — the very stage Jesus tells His listeners to walk away from.

his.t: Roman taxes and rich landowners made money a real worry for ordinary families.
Most families lived close to subsistence, so worry about food and clothing was daily reality.

cus.t: Pious Jews fasted twice a week, and some looked pale on purpose to be noticed.
Anointing the head with oil was normal grooming, so fasting should look ordinary.

cu: Pharisaic piety fasted twice weekly, often leaving faces deliberately pale and unwashed to advertise the discipline — the opposite of what Jesus instructs in v.17.

ot.n: Commands generosity toward the poor, background for the teaching on giving in v.1-4.
"Whoever is kind to the poor lends to the LORD" — the logic behind secret giving.
"Man looks at the outward appearance, but the LORD looks at the heart" — the verse underlying the whole chapter's contrast between public performance and private sincerity.

im.c: The Sermon on the Mount, by Gustave Doré (1866)

cm.n: Henry treats "treasure" broadly — not just money, but whatever the soul values most and rests its confidence in. He reads laying up treasure in heaven as tied directly to sincere giving, praying, and fasting done for God's eyes rather than a human audience, closing with his memorable point that where the treasure is, the heart cannot help but follow.

JFB dives into real scholarly disagreement over "daily bread" — the Greek word appears nowhere else in ancient literature, so its exact sense had to be reconstructed from its parts. They side with the majority reading, "bread sufficient for today's need," over the minority view that it means "bread for tomorrow," partly because the latter seems to contradict Jesus' own point…

On "seek first the kingdom of God," Wesley stresses the word first isn't about sequence but priority — not seeking the kingdom before other things and then moving on, but making it the single aim that reorders everything else. He notes that whoever truly seeks it first will, in time, come to seek it as the only thing that ultimately matters.

Lewis does not comment on Matthew 6 verse by verse, but his chapter "Forgiveness" in Mere Christianity begins with the line in the Lord's Prayer about forgiving those who trespass against us (v.12, 14-15). He says we cannot be forgiven unless we forgive, and that this is a hard saying, not an arbitrary one.

set: This chapter closes the Sermon on the Mount. Jesus is still early in His ministry, gathering disciples and redefining righteousness beyond the traditions of the scribes and Pharisees.

his.t: Preachers and would-be messiahs drew crowds in this era, so a test for false prophets mattered.
Scribes quoted earlier rabbis, but Jesus taught on His own authority.

cus.t: Walled towns had narrow gates, so the road through one was tight and easy to miss.
Sudden rains turned dry riverbeds into torrents that swept away poor foundations.

cu: Narrow city gates forced travelers to set down baggage before entering — a vivid image behind v.13-14. Sudden winter rains in the region could turn dry wadis into raging torrents, sweeping away homes without a solid foundation, the backdrop for the closing parable.

ot.n: "Do not hate your brother in your heart... rebuke your neighbor frankly" — background for the teaching on judgment.
Israel set before "life and death... choose life" — an early version of the two-ways image behind the narrow gate.
Paints the same two paths — one blessed, one perishing — that Jesus develops throughout this chapter.

im.c: The Sermon on the Mount, by Gustave Doré (1866)

cm.n: Henry reads "judge not" as forbidding us from sitting in a seat that isn't ours — we may judge our own actions, but not assume the authority to pronounce on someone else's heart or eternal state, since that belongs to God alone. He treats the wise and foolish builders as two audiences, not two doctrines: both hear the same sermon, but only one actually does what it says.

Clarke notes the Greek word order in v.6 is naturally reversed for clarity in translation — "dogs" pairs with "rend you" and "swine" with "trample underfoot," a common stylistic transposition in ancient writing. He also calls the Golden Rule the sum of everything the Law and Prophets teach about how people ought to treat one another.

Gill reads "pearls before swine" less as a blanket rule about withholding truth, and more as caution specifically about persistent, ill-natured rebuke — continuing to press correction on someone who has clearly shown no openness to receiving it, where the effort risks real loss and produces only hostility in return.

t: Authority Over Sickness, Storm, and Spirits
set: Capernaum sat on the Via Maris, a major trade route linking Egypt and Damascus, making it a bustling hub of both Jewish and Gentile life. Touching a leper technically violated the purity laws of Leviticus 13-14 — Jesus' willingness to do so is itself part of the account.

his.t: A centurion led about 100 soldiers and stood for the occupying power.
A garrison and customs town on a trade road, with Romans and Jews side by side.

cus.t: A healed leper brought offerings to the priest, as the Law of Moses required.
Banquet guests lay on couches, so "reclining with Abraham" pictures a feast of honor.

cu: A Roman centurion commanded roughly 80 soldiers and represented occupying military power — his approaching a Jewish teacher, and Jesus' willingness to help him, was a notable crossing of social lines. Pig herding, seen in the Gadarenes account, was common in the Decapolis, a largely Gentile region where pork was not a dietary restriction.

ot.n: The purification ritual for a healed leper, which Jesus tells the man to fulfill in v.4.
"He took up our infirmities and carried our diseases" — quoted directly as fulfilled in v.17.
God ruling over the seas and stilling storms — background for Jesus calming the storm in v.23-27.

im.c: Jesus Calming the Tempest, by Gustave Doré

cm.n: Henry draws out a quiet contrast: Moses' first recorded miracle was healing himself of leprosy, while Christ's early miracles are entirely for others' sake. On the storm, he notes this was the only time in the Gospels we read of Jesus sleeping — not from anxious exhaustion, but a serene, trusting rest, allowed to continue specifically to test the disciples' own faith while He…

JFB notes the leper's request is remarkably confident in substance yet humble in form — "if You are willing, You can" — certain of Jesus' power while leaving His willingness entirely open. They also observe this may well be the very first leper Jesus healed, since all three Synoptic Gospels record only this one case.

On "the Son of Man has nowhere to lay His head," Barnes draws a stark contrast: people of wealth and even open wickedness sleep on couches of ease, while the very foxes and birds have shelters of their own — yet the One who made them had no home and no pillow to call His own.

set: Only God was understood to have the authority to forgive sin (Isaiah 43:25, Psalm 103:3) — Jesus' declaration to the paralytic (v.2) is a direct claim to that divine prerogative.

his.t: They worked for Rome and were despised, so Jesus calling one was striking.
Local synagogue officials like Jairus held respected roles under Roman rule.

cus.t: Flat roofs of beams and clay could be opened, as when friends lowered the paralytic.
Flute players and wailing mourners were hired at a death, so they were already there.

cu: Friends lowering a paralyzed man to Jesus (implied by v.2, detailed further in Mark's parallel) reflects the common flat, mud-covered roof construction of Galilean homes. The bleeding woman's touch of Jesus' cloak fringe (v.20) refers to the tzitzit, tassels worn on the corners of a garment per Jewish law.

ot.n: God alone blots out transgressions — the claim implicit in Jesus forgiving sin in v.2.
"I desire mercy, not sacrifice" — quoted directly by Jesus in v.13.
The prophecy that the blind will see and the mute will speak in the day of salvation, echoed in v.27-33.

im.c: Jesus Raises the Daughter of Jairus, by Gustave Doré

cm.n: Henry treats forgiveness and healing as two sides of one act — sin, in his reading, is the deeper disease, and the physical cure is offered almost as visible proof that the invisible cure has already taken place.

JFB flags a genuine textual question worth knowing: the phrase "to repentance" at the end of v.13 has doubtful manuscript support here and in Mark's parallel, though it's undisputed in Luke's version of the same saying — the kind of small but real variant careful readers of old manuscripts have to weigh.

Gill leans into the physician metaphor directly — Jesus wasn't associating with tax collectors and sinners as a companion sharing their life, but as a doctor visiting the sick, which was not only lawful but commendable. The Pharisees, in his reading, weren't actually well; they simply didn't know themselves sick, which is precisely why they saw no need to come to Him.

set: Likely around AD 28-29, under Roman occupation. Jewish expectation of a conquering Messiah ran high — Jesus instead commissions unarmed, itinerant healers who preach repentance rather than revolt.

his.t: The mission began with Israel's own towns before reaching beyond them.
Synagogue courts could flog members, and Roman governors could try them.

cus.t: Traveling light made the Twelve depend on each town's hospitality.
Shaking dust from the feet marked leaving non-Jewish land, so here it was a solemn warning.

cu: Shaking dust off one's feet (v.14) was a rabbinic act normally used when leaving Gentile territory, to symbolize separation from defilement — using it against unwelcoming Jewish towns would have been a startling reversal. Synagogue leaders could legally administer up to 39 lashes (Deuteronomy 25:3), the punishment Jesus warns His disciples to expect in v.17.

ot.n: Family turned against family — quoted directly by Jesus in v.35-36.
The prophesied anointing to preach good news and set captives free, echoed in the mission Jesus gives the Twelve.
The legal limit of 39 lashes, the background for the synagogue floggings Jesus warns of in v.17.

im.c: He Sent Them Out Two by Two, by James Tissot (1886-1896)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry connects the number twelve directly to Israel's twelve tribes, casting the apostles as spiritual fathers meant to beget a new people for God. He also notes that the harshest warnings here — governors, kings, death itself — mostly outran what the Twelve actually faced on this first short mission; Jesus was preparing them for the far larger, harder commission still to come…

On shaking the dust off one's feet (v.14), JFB notes this kind of symbolic, wordless gesture was common across ancient cultures, not unique to Israel — and observes it's still practiced in parts of the world today as a way of visibly renouncing responsibility for how a message was received.

Barnes grounds the sparrow illustration in real, observed detail — sparrows in that region were common, small, and famously bold, nesting almost anywhere without any sense of belonging. His logic runs simply: if God attends even to creatures this ordinary and this cheap, His care for people made in His image runs deeper still.

set: John the Baptist is imprisoned at Machaerus, a fortress east of the Dead Sea, jailed by Herod Antipas for condemning his unlawful marriage. This chapter marks a turning point in Matthew's narrative — early excitement giving way to indecisive crowds and unmoved cities.

his.t: Herod Antipas had jailed John, so he asked his question from a cell.
Chorazin, Bethsaida and Capernaum were Jesus' main towns, and He warned them most.

cus.t: Village children played at weddings and funerals, the image Jesus uses for a stubborn crowd.
A yoke joined two animals to share a load, and teachers called their teaching a yoke.

cu: First-century village children mimicked weddings (with flutes) and funerals (with dirges) in play — the image Jesus uses in v.16-17 to describe a generation that refuses to respond to either John's austerity or His own joy.

ot.n: The promised messenger who prepares the way — quoted directly by Jesus about John in v.10.
The messianic signs Jesus lists in v.5 as proof of His identity to John.
The judgment on Sodom and on Tyre and Sidon, background for Jesus' comparisons in v.21-24.

im.c: Saint John the Baptist Sees Jesus from Afar, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry draws out the wordplay hidden in "rest" — Christ, he notes, is our true Noah, a name that itself means rest. He reads the yoke not as an added burden but a lighter one traded for a heavier: "you are under a yoke which makes you weary; shake that off and try mine, which will make you easy."

Clarke argues the Greek word translated "woe" is better read as "alas" — an exclamation of pity rather than a curse of wrath, changing the whole tone of Jesus' words toward these towns. He also notes the real irony of it: Bethsaida itself, one of the condemned towns, had already given the world three of the twelve apostles — Philip, Andrew, and Peter.

JFB points out that Capernaum's rebuke is sharper than Chorazin's or Bethsaida's precisely because it had more to lose — as the town where Jesus actually made His home throughout His Galilean ministry, it was, in their words, "the most favored spot upon earth," and its privilege only deepened its responsibility.

set: Galilee and Judea under Roman occupation (c. AD 28-30), where Pharisees emphasized strict Sabbath observance, oral tradition, and ritual purity. This chapter marks the point where opposition turns lethal — the Pharisees begin actively plotting Jesus' death (v.14).

his.t: Pharisees shaped village religious life and watched Jesus' Sabbath actions closely.
After the Sabbath healing, the Pharisees began plotting how to destroy Jesus.

cus.t: Pharisees counted plucking grain as reaping, work the Sabbath forbade.
Most rabbis allowed rescuing a sheep on the Sabbath, which Jesus uses in His answer.

cu: Pharisaic tradition counted the disciples' plucking grain as a form of "reaping," technically forbidden work on the Sabbath — Jesus responds by appealing to Scripture (David eating consecrated bread) rather than disputing the classification itself.

ot.n: David eating the consecrated bread — the precedent Jesus cites in v.3-4.
The Servant Song Matthew quotes almost verbatim in v.18-21.
Jonah's three days in the fish — the sign Jesus points to as a preview of His own burial and resurrection.

im.c: The Dumb Man Possessed, by Gustave Doré (1866)

cm.n: Henry has a memorable line for the name Beelzebub — literally "the god of a fly" or dunghill god — remarking on how far the accusation falls: "How art thou fallen, O Lucifer! from an angel of light, to be a lord of flies!

JFB calls Jesus' logic here "irresistible" — no divided kingdom, city, or household can stand for long, so the accusation that He casts out Satan by Satan's own power is simply incoherent on its own terms.

On the unpardonable sin, Clarke offers real pastoral reassurance: no one who genuinely believes in Jesus Christ's divine mission can actually commit it, so no troubled conscience needs to fear having already crossed that line by accident. The sin, in his reading, requires a settled, deliberate rejection, not an anxious doubt.

set: The Sea of Galilee's shoreline near Tabgha forms a natural amphitheater, and a boat becomes an instant pulpit for the large crowds gathering around Jesus. This chapter opens a new teaching block centered on "the kingdom of heaven," a phrase Matthew uses more than thirty times across his Gospel.

his.t: Most hearers were farmers or fishermen, so seeds and nets were familiar pictures.
Nazareth's people knew Jesus' family, which made His wisdom hard to accept.

cus.t: The weeds were likely darnel, which looks like wheat until it matures.
A mustard seed was proverbially tiny, yet the plant grew into a large shrub.

cu: The "weeds" in the parable of the weeds (v.24-30) are likely darnel, a plant that looks identical to wheat until mature — Roman law actually banned deliberately sowing darnel in an enemy's field, matching the malicious act Jesus describes.

ot.n: The prophecy of spiritual dullness Jesus quotes directly to explain why He teaches in parables.
"I will open My mouth in parables" — quoted directly in v.35 as fulfilled.
"The righteous will shine like the sun" — echoed in Jesus' explanation of the weeds in v.43.

im.c: Christ in the Synagogue, by Gustave Doré (1866)

cm.n: Henry reads the wheat-and-tares parable as a claim of ownership as much as a warning — "the world is Christ's field... whatever power and interest the devil has in it is usurped and unjust; when Christ comes to take possession, he comes whose right it is." He treats the mustard seed and leaven as two pictures of the same truth: the gospel's beginnings look small, but its end…

On the pearl of great price, Gill reads the merchant as Christ Himself, seeking out His elect — people who are precious to Him not because of any excellence in themselves, but purely because of the value He assigns them by His own grace, as His portion and inheritance.

On the hardened wayside soil, Clarke offers one of his more memorable lines: it pictures "a heart where Satan has ingress, egress, regress, and progress — in a word, the devil's thoroughfare." He's careful to note the unfruitfulness in the other soils isn't from bad seed or a careless sower, since the same seed is sown everywhere alike — the difference lies entirely in the…

set: Herod Antipas ruled Galilee and Perea (4 BC-AD 39) from his capital Tiberias, on the Sea of Galilee. His marriage to Herodias, his brother's wife, broke Leviticus 18:16 — John's public rebuke of that marriage is what led to his imprisonment and death.

his.t: Antipas married his brother's wife, and John's rebuke of it cost him his life.
Rulers' banquets drew officials and leaders, making Herod's oath a public one.

cus.t: A public oath was hard to break without losing face, so Herod gave the order.
The fourth watch came before dawn, so Jesus reached them in the last hours of night.

cu: Herod's oath, made rashly in front of dinner guests, obligated him by the social expectations of the time to honor it publicly even after regretting it — a dynamic Matthew highlights as a real constraint, not merely royal whim.

ot.n: The law against marrying a brother's wife, which John's rebuke of Herod was built on.
Elisha's smaller-scale bread multiplication miracle, a precedent for the feeding of the five thousand.
God described as treading on the sea and stilling storms — background for Jesus walking on water and calming the wind.

im.c: Christ Feeding the Multitude, by Gustave Doré

cm.n: Henry catches Herod's hollow, superstitious guilt precisely: "the devils believe and tremble, but they never believe and repent" — terror of conscience without any real change of heart. He also notes the timing isn't accidental: crowds pressed harder toward Jesus after John's martyrdom than before, since "the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church."

JFB catches a precise nuance in Peter's Greek that's easy to miss in translation — he doesn't ask Jesus to "let" him come, but to "command" him, using the language of an order rather than a permission. Read that way, his request looks less like impulsive boldness and more like a deliberate act of submission to whatever Jesus would say.

Clarke argues that when Jesus "blessed" the loaves, the object of that blessing was God Himself, not the bread — following standard Jewish custom of blessing the Giver rather than the gift. He also stresses the scale of the miracle plainly: five loaves fed five thousand men (plus women and children), with twelve baskets of fragments left over — more surplus than the entire…

set: By the first century, Pharisaic oral tradition (later written in the Mishnah) had grown into an extensive code — ceremonial hand-washing before meals was part of this tradition, not something commanded in the Law of Moses itself, which is the core of Jesus' challenge in v.1-9.

his.t: Pharisees guarded the Law with traditions handed down by elders, and Jesus questioned them.
Jews and their Phoenician neighbors shared trade and a long, uneasy history.

cus.t: Ritual hand washing before meals was a tradition, not a command of Moses.
Declaring money "Corban" set it aside for God, a loophole to avoid supporting parents.

cu: The "Corban" loophole (implied in v.5-6) allowed someone to declare money "devoted to God" and thereby legally withhold it from aging parents — a technically legal maneuver Jesus calls out as nullifying the actual command to honor one's father and mother.

ot.n: The command to honor father and mother, and the penalty for cursing them — both quoted directly by Jesus in v.4.
"These people honor Me with their lips" — quoted directly by Jesus in v.8-9.
Elisha's earlier, smaller-scale bread multiplication — a precedent for the feeding of the four thousand.

im.c: Jesus Healing the Sick, by Gustave Doré

cm.n: Henry is explicit that Jesus "doth not yet repeal the law of the distinction of meats (that was not done till Acts 10), but the tradition of the elders" — a mainstream 18th-century reading that lines up with the same distinction drawn in this chapter's own Translation notes: the dispute is about handwashing custom, not Levitical food law.

Barnes summarizes the whole passage in one clean line: "it is not the neglect of washing the body which defiles; it is the deep, inward corruption of the heart" — and lists evil thoughts first among the things that actually pollute a person, since thought precedes and produces every other named sin on Jesus' list.

On the Canaanite woman's reply, Ellicott offers a memorable reading: she "did not ask that the children might be deprived of any fragment of their portion; but taking her place, contentedly, among the dogs, she could still claim Him as her Master, and ask for the crumbs of His mercy."

set: Caesarea Philippi sat at the base of Mount Hermon, a region filled with pagan shrines, including a grotto dedicated to the god Pan — a strikingly public, idol-filled backdrop for Peter's confession of Jesus as "the Son of the living God." The Pharisees and Sadducees, normally opposed to each other, unite here in testing Jesus.

his.t: Herod's son Philip rebuilt it near a shrine to Pan, a center of pagan worship.
Many hoped for a warrior king to drive Rome out, so a suffering Messiah was hard to hear.

cus.t: A little yeast spreads through a whole batch of dough, which Jesus uses for false teaching.
Keys marked a steward's authority over a house, as in Isaiah 22.

cu: "Leaven" as a teaching metaphor (v.6-12) drew on something every listener understood physically — a small amount of yeast permeates an entire batch of dough, exactly how Jesus describes false teaching spreading quietly through a community.

ot.n: The Davidic covenant behind the title "Christ" Peter uses in his confession.
Jonah's three days in the fish — the sign Jesus again points to instead of a new miracle.
"The stone the builders rejected" — later applied to Jesus as the rock/cornerstone, connected to the imagery in v.18.

im.c: Get Thee Behind Me, Satan, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry is careful about what the "rock" actually is: "without doubt Christ himself is the Rock, the tried foundation of the church... Peter's confession is this rock as to doctrine" — the truth Peter spoke, not merely the man who spoke it, is what the church is built on.

On the keys, Bengel makes a precise textual observation: Jesus says "the keys of the kingdom of heaven," not "of the Church" and not "of the kingdoms of the world" — a deliberately narrower scope than later tradition sometimes assumed, tied specifically to admission into the kingdom itself.

Clarke reads the "leaven of the Pharisees and Sadducees" as false doctrine working exactly like literal leaven — quietly permeating and reshaping an entire mindset from within. He breaks "deny himself" into a deliberate progression: renouncing self-dependence, accepting whatever hardship following Christ brings, and imitating Jesus' own example step by step.

Lewis does not comment on Matthew 16, but his chapter "The Shocking Alternative" in Mere Christianity is about Peter's question in verses 13-16: who is Jesus? He argues against calling Jesus a great moral teacher while denying that He is God.

set: The unnamed "high mountain" is traditionally linked to Mount Tabor, though many scholars favor Mount Hermon, closer to Caesarea Philippi where the previous chapter's events took place. This occurs roughly six months before the crucifixion, under Roman rule with Herod Antipas governing Galilee.

his.t: Every adult Jewish man paid two drachmas a year toward temple upkeep.
Capernaum lay in Herod Antipas' Galilee, where tolls and taxes were collected.

cus.t: Peter's offer of shelters recalls the booths built at the Feast of Tabernacles.
A stater was a silver coin worth four drachmas, enough for two men's temple tax.

cu: The two-drachma temple tax (v.24) was an annual payment expected of every adult Jewish male to support temple upkeep, based on Exodus 30:13-16 — Jesus' point about "sons" being exempt from a king's tax makes a claim about His own identity before He agrees to pay anyway.

ot.n: Moses' face shining after meeting with God — the visual precedent for Jesus' transfiguration.
The cloud, mountain, and voice at Sinai, paralleling the Transfiguration's setting.
The promise of Elijah's return before the Day of the Lord, discussed by Jesus and the disciples in v.10-13.

im.c: The Transfiguration, by Gustave Doré (1866)

cm.n: Henry reads the moment the vision fades — "they saw no man, save Jesus only" — as the whole point condensed into five words: whatever authority Moses and Elijah carried as prophets, they were willing to see it entirely transferred to Christ, whose silence at "hear him" was itself their consent.

JFB draws a precise distinction most readers miss: the temple tax in this chapter was an ecclesiastical due, not a civil tax like the one debated with Caesar's coin later in chapter 22 — and they argue the whole force of Jesus' reasoning about kings not taxing their own children depends on keeping that distinction clear.

Gill notes that "faith as a grain of mustard seed" wasn't an image Jesus invented on the spot — it was already a known proverbial phrase in Jewish sources for describing something impossibly small in quantity, which makes Jesus' point sharper: even that little is enough.

set: In first-century Judea, children held essentially no social status — placing a child at the literal center of the discussion in v.2 upends the disciples' assumptions about greatness before Jesus says a word.

his.t: Unpaid debt could send a family to prison or slavery, so the servant's fate was real.
Tax collectors and Gentiles were kept at a distance, so "treat him like one" meant exclusion.

cus.t: Children had no status in the ancient world, so honoring one was a shock.
A donkey millstone was massive, so being drowned with one was a terrifying image.

cu: Millstones (v.6) were massive circular stones, typically turned by a donkey, far too heavy to be a casual image — the horror of being drowned with one tied to the neck is the entire point. Legal disputes in Israel were customarily settled by private discussion first, then escalated to two or three witnesses per Deuteronomy 19:15, the exact process Jesus outlines in v.15-17.

ot.n: The two-or-three-witnesses principle Jesus applies directly to church conflict in v.16.
Lamech's boast of sevenfold, then seventy-sevenfold revenge — reversed by Jesus into a command for limitless forgiveness.
God's rebuke of shepherds who neglect and harm the flock, background for the warnings about "little ones" in v.6-10.

im.c: Parable of the Unforgiving Servant, by Claude Vignon (17th century)

cm.n: Henry notes Peter's proposed cap on forgiveness — seven times — already sounded generous to him, likely drawing on Proverbs 24:16's "a just man falls seven times." Jesus' answer isn't a new, larger number to count toward, but a refusal to count at all: "it does not look well for us to keep count of the offences done against us."

Clarke does the actual math on the unforgiving servant's debt: ten thousand talents of gold would equal roughly £67.5 million sterling — by his reckoning, equal to the entire annual revenue of the British Empire in his own day.

Barnes grounds the millstone image in real detail — the Greek specifies the large kind turned by a mule or donkey, not the small handheld sort, making the punishment described genuinely severe rather than a loose figure of speech.

Lewis does not comment on Matthew 18, but his chapter "Forgiveness" in Mere Christianity is a close companion to the parable of the unforgiving servant (v.21-35). He says forgiving is easy to admire in theory and hard when it is a particular person who has wronged us.

set: Jesus has left Galilee for Judea, in the region of Perea under Herod Antipas. The Pharisees' question about divorce (v.3) drops Him into a live rabbinic debate between the schools of Hillel (permitting divorce for almost any reason) and Shammai (permitting it only for sexual immorality) — Jesus sidesteps both schools by…

his.t: Rabbis argued over grounds for divorce, from only adultery to almost any reason.
Many saw wealth as a sign of God's favor, so the disciples were shocked.

cus.t: A husband gave a written divorce certificate, which let the wife remarry.
The camel was the largest animal in Galilee, so the image is deliberately absurd.

cu: Divorce certificates (get) and marriage contracts (ketubot) from this era are attested in surviving first-century papyri, confirming the legal practice Jesus is questioned about. Patriarchs traditionally blessed children by laying hands on them (as in Genesis 48:14) — the custom the parents in v.13 are seeking from Jesus.

ot.n: The creation account Jesus quotes directly as the foundation for His teaching on marriage.
The Mosaic divorce provision the Pharisees cite, which Jesus reframes as a concession rather than the ideal.
The commandments Jesus lists to the rich young man, drawn directly from the Law.

im.c: Christ and the Rich Young Ruler, by Heinrich Hofmann

cm.n: Henry extends the camel image with real feeling: a rich man, he says, is fittingly compared to a camel because he carries his wealth the way a camel carries its load — it isn't truly his, he received it from others, spends it for others, and must shortly leave it to others.

JFB is precise about where Jesus grounds His teaching on marriage: not in later Mosaic regulation, but in "the original constitution of man as one pair, a male and a female," by God's own design at creation — the divorce debate, in their reading, was never really about interpreting a loophole, but about which starting point defines marriage in the first place.

Gill reads the Pharisees' motive plainly: they came not for the sake of learning, but as spies, watching for any opportunity to expose Jesus to public hatred. On Moses' divorce provision, he draws a careful distinction — it was God permitting an accommodation through Moses' civil law, not God's own original design, which is exactly the difference Jesus presses in His answer.

t: A Parable, a Prediction, and a Request
set: Day laborers in this era gathered in village marketplaces before dawn hoping to be hired for the day — a standard workday ran roughly 6am to 6pm, and any day without work meant no food. Jesus' landowner returning four separate times (9am, noon, 3pm, 5pm) to keep hiring reflects unusual, deliberate generosity.

his.t: Landless workers waited in the marketplace each day hoping to be hired.
Roman governors and client kings ruled by force, the model Jesus contrasts with serving.

cus.t: A denarius was a day's wage for a laborer.
The day counted from sunrise, so the eleventh hour was near sunset.

cu: A denarius (v.2) was the standard daily wage for unskilled labor — Roman coins bearing Tiberius Caesar's image from this exact period have been recovered by archaeologists, confirming the coin's use and value.

ot.n: The vineyard as an image for God's people, background for the parable's central setting.
The concept of a ransom price paid for a life, echoed directly in v.28.
The suffering servant bearing the guilt of "many" — closely echoed in Jesus' description of His own coming death.

im.c: Parable of the Laborers in the Vineyard, by Rembrandt

cm.n: Henry reads the parable's core point as a correction, not a contradiction: the reward for a life of service isn't wages earned by the hour, but a gift given by grace — "not as wages for the value of their work, but as the gift of God." To the grumbling laborer, the master's answer is simple: you received exactly what you agreed to; his generosity elsewhere took nothing from…

Spurgeon notes the emotional turn in the early workers' reaction: they had exactly what was promised, a fair wage, freely agreed to — yet "as soon as the penny was in their hand, a murmur was in their mouth." Their only real grievance, he observes dryly, was that the master had been too generous to those who worked less.

Wesley works out the actual value of a day's wage for his own 18th-century readers: the Roman penny (denarius) equaled roughly fourteen cents in his era's money — a modest but real sum, making the landowner's generosity to the last-hired workers genuinely costly, not merely symbolic.

set: Passover week drew enormous crowds into Jerusalem — possibly over a million pilgrims. The route from Bethphage descends the Mount of Olives ridge into a sweeping view of the city and Temple Mount, making Jesus' entry a deliberate, public declaration rather than a quiet arrival.

his.t: Pilgrims filled Jerusalem for Passover, ready to cheer a king.
The temple ran on Tyrian silver, so money changers worked in the courts.

cus.t: A king on a donkey meant peace, not war, unlike a king on a war horse.
Spreading cloaks and branches on the road honored a king.

cu: Money changers in the temple's Court of the Gentiles swapped ordinary coins for the Tyrian silver required for temple offerings, often at exploitative rates — the commerce Jesus overturns had effectively taken over the one court where non-Jews were permitted to pray.

ot.n: The prophecy of a gentle king riding a donkey, quoted directly and fulfilled in v.5.
The two prophetic texts Jesus combines in His rebuke during the temple cleansing.
"The stone the builders rejected" — quoted directly by Jesus at the close of the parable of the tenants.

im.c: Christ's Entry into Jerusalem, by Gustave Doré (1866)

cm.n: Henry reads the fig tree as a picture of hypocrisy in general — leaves without fruit, a plausible show without real substance, which withers as soon as it's tested. He draws a pointed, sobering connection forward: how quickly the nation's own "fig tree" would wither after the crowd's cry a few days later, "His blood be on us, and our children."

MacArthur frames the temple cleansing and the fig tree's cursing as two connected acts of the same sovereign authority — one denouncing corrupted religion, the other denouncing a fruitless nation. He notes that Matthew compresses two mornings (the cursing and the discovery of it withered) into one continuous account, a common and accepted way ancient historians told a story.

Gill notes that Bethphage itself means 'house of figs,' named for the fig trees covering that stretch of the Mount of Olives — which makes it a striking detail that Jesus' triumphal entry begins from a place named for figs, just two days before He curses a fig tree found full of leaves but no fruit nearby.

set: This chapter takes place entirely within the temple courts during the final week before the crucifixion. Tension is at its peak — religious leaders sense their authority slipping in front of the crowds and escalate from questioning to open entrapment attempts.

his.t: Pharisees, Herodians and Sadducees disagreed on much, yet teamed up to trap Jesus.
Many Jews hated paying tax to Caesar, so the question was a trap.

cus.t: Guests were expected to dress properly for a wedding feast, as a sign of respect.
A childless widow married her husband's brother to carry on the family line.

cu: A Roman denarius (v.19) bore Tiberius Caesar's image and an inscription naming him "son of the divine Augustus" — showing such a coin inside the temple was itself provocative, which is exactly why Jesus asks them to produce one rather than producing it Himself.

ot.n: The levirate marriage law the Sadducees cite in their trick question about the resurrection.
The two Old Testament commands Jesus names as the greatest — love of God and love of neighbor.
"The LORD said to my Lord" — quoted directly by Jesus in His closing question about the Messiah's identity.

im.c: Christ and the Tribute Money, by Gustave Doré

cm.n: Henry catches a subtlety in the word "render": Jesus doesn't say "give" Caesar his coin, but "render" or "restore" it — acknowledging it was already Caesar's by virtue of whose image it bore. He sums up the whole answer in one line: "if our purses be Caesar's, our consciences are God's."

On the wedding garment, Clarke draws in real ancient custom: it was standard at Near Eastern and Greek celebrations for the host to provide festive robes for guests, so the man without one had no excuse — he could have simply asked for one.

Gill grounds the wedding parable in real Jewish custom: fathers traditionally paid for and hosted their son's marriage feast — he cites the rabbinic principle directly, 'a father marries his son, and makes a feast for him, and the expense is the father's.' The king in the parable is following an ordinary, recognizable social pattern, not an invented scenario.

set: Almost certainly Tuesday of Passion Week, in the temple courts, immediately after Jesus has silenced every group that tried to trap Him in chapter 22. This is His last public teaching before the Olivet Discourse and His arrest.

his.t: Scribes and Pharisees were respected teachers, which made Jesus' public rebuke striking.
Jerusalem had a history of killing prophets, which Jesus names.

cus.t: Small leather boxes of Scripture were worn on the arm and forehead, and some wore showy ones.
Tombs were whitewashed so travelers wouldn't touch them and become unclean.

cu: Phylacteries — small leather boxes containing Scripture passages, bound to the arm and forehead per Deuteronomy 6:4-9 — and tassels (tzitzit) worn on garment corners per Numbers 15:38 were genuine, commanded religious practices. Jesus' critique isn't the practices themselves but leaders enlarging them for visible display.

ot.n: The murder of Abel — the opening act of righteous bloodshed Jesus references in v.35.
The murder of Zechariah son of Jehoiada "between the temple and the altar" — the closing act of bloodshed Jesus references.
"Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord" — the words Jesus says Jerusalem will one day cry out, closing His lament in v.39.

im.c: The Pharisees Question Jesus, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry reads the whole chapter as showing outward religion dressed up over inward rot — "the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees was like the ornaments of a grave, or dressing up a dead body, only for show." He notes the self-deceiving irony of v.30: they build monuments honoring prophets their own ancestors killed, never suspecting they're about to repeat the pattern.

JFB adds a vivid, timely detail: Jewish custom whitewashed tombs on a fixed day each year, specifically to make them more visible so pilgrims wouldn't accidentally touch one and become ceremonially unclean.

Gill unpacks 'mercy' as 'all acts of compassion to the distressed, relieving the necessitous, distributing to their wants' — precisely the practical, hands-on kindness he says the Pharisees 'very little practised, being a set of cruel, hard hearted, and covetous persons' beneath their meticulous tithing of garden herbs.

t: The Return of the Son of Man
set: It's likely Tuesday of Passion Week. Jesus has just left the magnificently rebuilt temple — its white marble and gold famous throughout the region — and sits on the Mount of Olives, which offers a direct, sweeping view back across the Kidron Valley to the temple He has just predicted will fall.

his.t: Its gleaming stone and gold made the idea of its fall seem unthinkable.
Rome destroyed the temple in AD 70, about forty years later.

cus.t: Flat roofs were living space with outside stairs, so fleeing meant not going back inside.
Travel on the Sabbath was limited, which would make a Sabbath flight harder.

cu: Flat rooftops (v.17) were used as everyday living space, reachable by an external staircase — Jesus' warning pictures someone fleeing so urgently they don't even go back down inside the house first, grabbing nothing on the way out.

ot.n: The "abomination of desolation" language Jesus quotes directly and tells His disciples to understand by returning to Daniel.
Cosmic darkening imagery — sun, moon, and stars — echoed in Jesus' description of the tribulation's aftermath.
The "Son of Man" coming on the clouds with authority — the image Jesus directly applies to Himself in v.30.

im.c: The Prophecy of the Destruction of the Temple, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Wesley notes the weight of the moment often gets lost in a familiar story: this was the last time Jesus ever entered the temple. He "took his final leave of it, never to return more to it" — the prediction of its destruction wasn't abstract prophecy from a distance, but His parting words on walking out the door for good.

Gill reads the disciples' admiration of the temple's stones and buildings as revealing exactly what Jesus is about to challenge — they were, in his words, "intent on the outward splendour, and worldly grandeur" of the structure, finding it almost unbelievable that something built so massive and firm could ever actually fall.

Clarke offers a linguistic note on v.36: the Greek word translated 'hour' was also used by both biblical and secular ancient writers to mean 'season' more broadly — worth knowing when weighing exactly how precise a timeframe the verse is actually claiming is unknown.

t: The Ten Virgins, the Talents, the Sheep and Goats
set: Still Passover week, with the same private setting as chapter 24. Each of the three teachings answers the same underlying question from the disciples: what does it look like to actually be ready when the master returns?

his.t: Days before Passover, Jesus teaches in Jerusalem while the leaders look for a way to arrest Him.
Wealthy men often left money in the care of trusted slaves, so the parable was familiar.

cus.t: Small clay lamps burned only a short while, so spare oil was needed.
A talent was a huge sum, roughly many years of a laborer's pay.

cu: First-century village weddings had the groom fetch the bride from her father's house at night, with attendants lighting the way using small olive-oil lamps that burned only 15-30 minutes before needing more fuel — explaining exactly why the "wise" virgins carried an extra flask and the "foolish" ones didn't.

ot.n: God separating "fat" sheep from "lean" sheep in judgment — background imagery for the sheep and goats scene.
God pictured rejoicing over His people like a bridegroom — background for the wedding imagery in the ten virgins.
The Son of Man receiving glory and authority to judge — directly echoed in v.31 as Jesus describes His own return.

im.c: Parable of the Wise and Foolish Virgins, by Hieronymus Francken the Younger (c. 1616)

cm.n: Henry explains a detail easy to miss: ten wasn't a random number for the parable's bridesmaids — Jewish custom generally required at least ten people present for a synagogue service, a circumcision, a Passover, or a wedding (as when Boaz married Ruth with ten witnesses). The parable's math is drawn straight from real social practice, not invented for the story.

Clarke reads the choice of animals itself as meaningful: sheep have long been considered emblems of mildness, simplicity, patience, and usefulness, while goats carried the opposite associations in ancient thought — the imagery itself, familiar to any first-century listener with flocks, was already doing some of the teaching before a word of explanation was given.

Gill notes the custom behind the parable was genuinely widespread, not unique to Jewish practice: meeting the bridegroom at night and escorting him home by lamplight was shared by other ancient eastern peoples as well — the scene would have needed no explanation to Jesus' listeners.

Lewis does not comment on Matthew 25, but his sermon "The Weight of Glory" speaks to verse 40, "whatever you did for one of the least of these." He says there are no ordinary people: you have never talked to a mere mortal, and the person next to you is either a creature headed for glory or one headed for something terrible.

set: Passover in Jerusalem, with the city swollen by pilgrims and Roman troops watching closely. The chief priests, gathered at Caiaphas' residence, explicitly fear a riot if they move against Jesus publicly during the feast — a fear that shapes their entire secretive plan.

his.t: Jerusalem swelled with pilgrims who came to remember the exodus.
Caiaphas was high priest from AD 18 to 36 and worked closely with Rome.

cus.t: At Passover guests reclined at table, so a dipped bowl was shared closely.
Several cups of wine were drunk during the Passover meal.

cu: Reclining at table (v.20) was the customary posture for a formal meal, especially Passover — guests ate lying on one side, propped on an elbow, which is why "dipping into the bowl" together (v.23) was physically close enough to identify a specific person.

ot.n: The thirty pieces of silver, thrown to a potter — fulfilled precisely in Judas' payment and later disposal of the money.
"I will strike the Shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered" — quoted directly by Jesus in v.31.
"Even my close friend...has lifted up his heel against me" — the betrayal-by-a-trusted-companion pattern echoed in Judas' act.

im.c: Jesus Praying in the Garden, by Gustave Doré (1866)

cm.n: Henry translates the name Gethsemane directly — an olive press, a place where olives were crushed under weight to yield their oil — a name that becomes almost unbearably fitting for what happens there. He also captures Judas's audacity in one striking line, imagining Jesus' unspoken thought as the traitor approaches face to face: "do you betray me to my very face?"

Clarke notes thirty pieces of silver wasn't an arbitrary sum — it was the exact legal compensation fixed in Exodus 21:32 for a slave gored to death by someone else's ox. The chief priests, whether they intended it or not, valued Jesus at precisely the price of the lowest, most replaceable life the law recognized.

Gill surveys the range of ways 'cup' was used as an image in that era — a physician's dose given to a patient, a poison given to condemn a criminal, or simply the portion a host allotted each guest at a meal.

set: Roman governors alone held authority over capital punishment, which is why the chief priests must hand Jesus to Pilate rather than execute Him themselves. Pilate's headquarters was likely the Antonia Fortress, adjoining the temple.

his.t: Pilate governed Judea from AD 26 to 36 and was known for harsh rule.
Rome used crucifixion to punish rebels and slaves as a public warning.

cus.t: A prisoner was released at the festival, a gesture to calm the crowds.
Bodies were wrapped in cloth and laid in rock-cut tombs sealed with a stone.

cu: It was the governor's custom to release one prisoner chosen by the crowd at Passover (v.15) — a practice not confirmed outside the Gospels but consistent with Rome's general strategy of small conciliatory gestures toward occupied populations during volatile religious festivals.

ot.n: The rejected shepherd's wages thrown "to the potter" — echoed in the chief priests' use of Judas' returned silver to buy the potter's field.
An extraordinarily detailed psalm of suffering — mocking, divided garments, and the cry of abandonment are all echoed directly in the crucifixion scene.
The suffering servant "assigned a grave with the rich" — fulfilled in Jesus' burial in Joseph of Arimathea's own tomb.

im.c: Crucifixion of Jesus, by Gustave Doré (1866)

cm.n: Henry catches the strange logic of Pilate's hand-washing: "what nonsense was this, to condemn him, and yet protest that he was innocent of his blood" — declaring innocence while actively signing the death warrant anyway.

Johnson's People's New Testament commentary offers a precise linguistic note on the centurion's confession: as a Roman soldier raised in a polytheistic world, his Greek words more literally mean "a son of a god" rather than "the Son of God" in the full Christian sense — remarkable testimony from a pagan witness, even without later doctrinal precision behind it.

Gill notes Barabbas is called 'notable' in a double sense — famous or rather infamous, a known thief, insurrectionist, and murderer, someone 'deserving of death' by any standard. He reads Pilate's framing of the choice — Barabbas or 'Jesus, who is called the Christ' — as deliberately setting the worst possible contrast, expecting the crowd to obviously choose Jesus.
Lewis does not comment on Matthew 27, but his chapter "The Perfect Penitent" in Mere Christianity asks what the crucifixion accomplished. He says the fact matters more than any one theory about it.

set: Dawn on the first day of the week — Sunday, following the Sabbath rest. Roman guard units assigned to a tomb typically numbered four to sixteen soldiers; falling asleep on duty carried the death penalty, which explains why they needed a substantial bribe to accept blame for an empty tomb.

his.t: Pilate allowed a guard and a sealed stone to prevent theft of the body.
Leaders spread the claim that the disciples stole the body, still repeated when Matthew wrote.

cus.t: Women's testimony carried little weight in court, yet they are first at the tomb.
Spices and perfumes were brought to honor the body, not to preserve it.

cu: Women preparing to visit and anoint a body (implied here, explicit in the other Gospels) reflects standard first-century burial custom — visiting a tomb on the third day was also common practice, intended to confirm death had truly occurred.

ot.n: The Son of Man receiving all authority, glory, and an everlasting kingdom — directly echoed in Jesus' declaration in v.18.
God's promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham's offspring — finding its fulfillment in the Great Commission's reach to "all nations."
"You will not abandon my soul to Sheol" — read by the early church as a resurrection prophecy fulfilled in this chapter.

im.c: The Angel at the Sepulcher, by Gustave Doré (1866)

cm.n: Henry sees deliberate design in a small detail people often skip past: God ordered it so that witnesses would see Christ risen, but not actually see him rise — the same principle, he notes, that governed the incarnation itself, "a mystery...

On the soldiers' bribed cover story, Henry notes it had remarkable staying power — citing Justin Martyr's record that the Jewish authorities were still circulating this same fabricated "stolen body" explanation to Jewish communities abroad decades later, treating it as a deliberate, sustained campaign rather than a one-time lie.

Gill makes a careful grammatical point about 'teach all nations, baptizing them': in the Greek, 'them' doesn't grammatically match 'all nations' (a neuter noun) but rather 'disciples,' implied by the verb 'make disciples' just before it — meaning the command is to baptize those actually taught and won as disciples, not indiscriminately baptize entire populations.

set: Mark opens with no birth narrative at all — a deliberate choice, plunging straight into John the Baptist and Jesus' baptism. Capernaum, on the Sea of Galilee's northwest shore, quickly becomes the operational base for everything that follows in this chapter.

his.t: Rome ruled Judea through a governor, and many Jews longed for freedom.
Galilean fishermen often worked in family crews and owned boats.

cus.t: Camel hair and a leather belt recalled the prophet Elijah.
Teachers usually quoted earlier rabbis, but Jesus spoke on His own authority.

cu: Rabbis of this era typically taught by citing the chain of earlier teachers behind a given interpretation. Jesus notably doesn't — He teaches directly, in His own voice, which is exactly what the astonished crowd in the Capernaum synagogue immediately picks up on.

ot.n: The promised messenger preparing the way — quoted directly in v.2.
"A voice calling in the wilderness" — quoted directly in v.3, identifying John's role.
Elijah's rough, hairy garment — the model behind John's own camel-hair clothing, hinting he's the promised Elijah-like forerunner.

im.c: John the Baptist Preaching in the Wilderness, by Gustave Doré (1866)

cm.n: Gill draws out the significance of Jesus physically touching the leper in v.41 — under the Law, touching a leper made a person ceremonially unclean, and no ordinary person would have risked it.

Henry points out that unlike Matthew and Luke, Mark skips the nativity entirely and opens with John's ministry — treating this, not the birth, as the actual "beginning of the gospel." He observes that the chapter's two Old Testament quotations, from Malachi and Isaiah, were written roughly three centuries apart yet both point to this exact same moment.

JFB highlights Mark's characteristic abruptness — skipping everything that came before to plunge straight into John's ministry, as if impatient to reach Jesus's public life. They make an interesting observation: despite being the shortest of the four Gospels overall, Mark is often the fullest and most detailed in the specific scenes it does choose to include.

set: Capernaum again, likely at Peter's own house, packed so tightly that four men resort to digging through the roof. First-century Galilean homes used flat roofs made of branches, mud, and packed earth over wooden beams — genuinely possible to open up from above without structural danger.

his.t: They worked for Rome and were hated as collaborators who took extra.
It sat on a trade road, so tax collectors set up booths there.

cus.t: Roofs of beams, branches and clay could be opened from above.
Old skins grew stiff and would burst if filled with fermenting wine.

cu: Pharisaic tradition had expanded fasting well beyond the Day of Atonement into a twice-weekly practice. Jesus' bridegroom imagery would have been immediately understood as a wedding metaphor — wedding guests were specifically exempted from fasting obligations during the celebration itself.

ot.n: God alone blots out transgressions — the theological principle behind the scribes' objection in v.7.
David eating the consecrated bread when hungry — the precedent Jesus cites directly in v.25-26.
The Sabbath's origin at creation and its place in the Ten Commandments — background for Jesus' claim of Lordship over it.

im.c: The Disciples Plucking Corn on the Sabbath, by Gustave Doré (1866)

cm.n: Henry reads Jesus' choice to forgive before healing as deliberate: "pardon of sin strikes at the root of all diseases," since sin is, in his words, the true disease of the soul. The physical healing becomes almost secondary — a visible sign of the deeper, invisible work Jesus had already done.

JFB notes something easy to miss: all three Gospel accounts specifically say Jesus saw "their faith" — not just the paralyzed man's, but his four friends' as well. It was a shared, active faith, one that pushed through a crowded doorway and tore open a roof rather than accepting defeat.

Calvin frames the whole miracle as a kind of proof by demonstration — since forgiveness itself can't be visibly tested, Christ intentionally paired His invisible claim to forgive sins with a visible, undeniable sign (the healing) to confirm and seal an authority that could otherwise only be taken on faith.

Lewis does not comment on Mark 2, but "The Shocking Alternative" in Mere Christianity centers on Jesus' words to the paralytic, "Your sins are forgiven" (v.5-10). Lewis says that anyone can forgive a wrong done to himself, but a man who forgives wrongs done to other people is making an absurd claim unless he is the one whom every sin offends.

set: The healing opens in a synagogue, almost certainly Capernaum's again. The crowd that follows in v.7-8 comes from a strikingly wide geographic spread — Galilee, Judea, Jerusalem, Idumea (Edom, south of Judea), across the Jordan, and even the Gentile coastal cities of Tyre and Sidon.

his.t: Supporters of Herod's family, usually rivals of the Pharisees.
People came from Judea, Idumea, across the Jordan and Tyre and Sidon.

cus.t: Many rabbis allowed healing on the Sabbath only to save a life.
Family was a person's greatest loyalty, so Jesus' words shocked.

cu: Pharisees and Herodians were natural political rivals — Herodians supported Rome's client king, while Pharisees resented foreign rule. Their willingness to conspire together against Jesus (v.6) shows just how seriously His growing authority was being taken.

ot.n: King Jeroboam's hand withers and is later restored — a precedent for God's power over a rebellious hand.
The twelve pillars representing Israel's twelve tribes — background for Jesus choosing exactly twelve apostles.
"Woe to those who call evil good and good evil" — echoed in the scribes' inversion of Jesus' Spirit-empowered work as demonic.

im.c: The Man with the Withered Hand, by James Tissot (1886-1894)
im.k: Public domain — Brooklyn Museum / Wikimedia Commons

cm.n: Henry draws a spiritual parallel from the physical healing: "our hands are spiritually withered, the powers of our souls weakened by sin, and disabled for that which is good" — the same healing power at work in the synagogue that day is what's needed for the soul.

Jerome preserves a detail from an early, non-canonical Gospel used by two ancient Jewish-Christian groups: it names the man's trade, describing him praying, "I was a builder, and gained my living by the labour of my hands; I pray thee, Jesus, to restore me to health, that I may not disgracefully beg my bread." This isn't part of Scripture itself, but it shows how early…

The 8th-century English monk Bede reads the healing allegorically: 'Adam plucking the forbidden fruit dried up the hand of the human race, depriving man of the power to be fruitful in good works. Christ, however, restored that power by stretching forth His hands on the cross.' A withered hand restored becomes, in his reading, a picture of humanity itself restored.

set: The Sea of Galilee's shoreline acts as a natural amphitheater, and teaching from a boat gave Jesus both distance from the crush of the crowd and a way for His voice to carry across the water to the shore.

his.t: Most listeners lived by farming and fishing, so seeds and nets were everyday pictures.
Cold air off the hills can whip up sudden storms on the lake.

cus.t: Farmers scattered seed by hand before plowing it under.
The curved shore works like an amphitheater, carrying a voice across the water.

cu: Galilean farmers scattered seed by hand before plowing, meaning some inevitably landed on hardened footpaths, thin soil over limestone shelf, or ground still thick with thornbush roots — every detail in the parable would have matched something the crowd could see from where they stood.

ot.n: Seeing without perceiving, hearing without understanding — quoted directly by Jesus to explain His use of parables.
Sailors crying out to God in a storm, who then stills the wind and waves — the same pattern Jesus enacts in v.39.
A great tree sheltering birds in its branches — background imagery echoed directly in the mustard seed parable.

im.c: Jesus Calming the Tempest, by Gustave Doré

cm.n: Henry pictures the sower scattering seed indiscriminately, quoting Ecclesiastes 11:1's image of sowing "beside all waters" — the word of God given out to everyone alike, not knowing in advance where it will land or what it will produce. Ministers, he says, are sowers in the same pattern, not judges of the soil.

JFB points out something the text leaves deliberately open: Jesus never actually identifies who the sower is. They read this as intentional — since the seed is the word of God, anyone who scatters that word, in any generation, can be understood as a sower in the same parable, not just Jesus Himself.

Ryle writes with real force about the storm-calming: 'He speaks to the waves, and they submit to His command. He turns the raging storm into a calm with a few words — 'Peace, be still.' The elements knew the voice of their Master, and, like obedient servants, were quiet at once.' No stormy passion, he adds, is too strong for the same Christ to tame.

set: The eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee, in Gentile territory — the region of the Gerasenes sat within the Decapolis, ten largely Greek-influenced cities. A large pig herd (unthinkable in Jewish territory, since pigs were unclean under Mosaic law) instantly signals this is Gentile land.

his.t: A league of ten Greek cities east of Galilee, where Gentiles lived.
A Roman legion was five to six thousand soldiers.

cus.t: Hillside caves served as tombs, and touching the dead made one unclean.
A woman with a flow of blood was ritually unclean and kept apart.

cu: Tombs were natural, cave-like dwellings cut into hillsides, and dwelling among them made a person ritually unclean on top of whatever affliction they already carried. A Roman legion typically numbered five to six thousand soldiers — the demon's chosen name signals overwhelming, organized spiritual occupation, not a single affliction.

ot.n: Pigs declared unclean under the Law — background for the herd's presence confirming this is Gentile territory.
God breaking chains and freeing prisoners from darkness — echoed in the deliverance of the chained demoniac.
Elisha raising a child from death in a private room — a precedent for Jesus raising Jairus's daughter with only a few witnesses present.

im.c: Jesus Raises the Daughter of Jairus, by Gustave Doré

cm.n: Henry draws a deliberate contrast between the chapter's two petitioners: Jairus comes openly, publicly falling at Jesus' feet as a respected synagogue ruler, while the bleeding woman comes clandestinely, hoping to "steal" a cure unnoticed in the crush of the crowd.

On the mourners who laugh at Jesus for saying the girl is only "sleeping," Henry notes their scorn actually strengthens the case for the miracle rather than weakening it — their reaction proves beyond dispute that everyone present, including the family, genuinely believed the child was dead.

Ryle draws out a lesson from Jairus's status: 'rank places no man beyond the reach of sorrow. Jairus was a ruler; yet sickness and trouble came to his house.' On the raising itself, he writes plainly: 'the keys of death are in our Lord Jesus Christ's hands' — a power no synagogue office or social standing could have purchased.

set: Nazareth was a small, close-knit Galilean village of likely fewer than 500 residents — everyone genuinely did know Jesus' family, which is precisely what makes their unbelief so pointed. The chapter's flashback to John's death likely took place at Machaerus, Herod Antipas's desert fortress east of the Dead Sea.

his.t: He ruled Galilee and jailed John for criticizing his marriage.
A small village of farmers and craftsmen, so a hometown teacher was hard to take seriously.

cus.t: Shaking dust off one's feet signaled a break with a town.
A king could not easily take back a vow made in front of guests.

cu: Shaking dust from one's feet (v.11) mirrored the practice of Jewish travelers symbolically removing pagan soil upon returning home — using the gesture against fellow Israelites was a pointed warning. Herod's birthday banquet, with its rash public oath before nobles and commanders, reflects the kind of honor-bound promise a king of that era couldn't easily walk back without losing face.

ot.n: The law against marrying a brother's wife — the basis of John's rebuke of Herod.
"Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?" — directly answered by the feeding of the five thousand.
God alone "treads on the waves of the sea" — the exact authority Jesus displays by walking on water.

im.c: Jesus Walks on the Sea, by Gustave Doré

cm.n: Henry notes the grim irony in Herod's guilty conscience: "he feared John while he lived, and now, when he thought he had got clear of him, fears him ten times worse when he is dead." He observes this is a case of "the terrors of strong conviction, where there is not the truth of a saving conversion" — real fear of God without real repentance.

On the feeding miracle, Henry notes Jesus didn't delegate the blessing to a disciple but "craved" it Himself before the bread multiplied — and observes that the crowd, unlike the disciples who wanted to send everyone away hungry, never once asked to leave, since they "esteemed the words of Christ's mouth more than their necessary food."

Ryle draws out 'the amazing power of truth over the conscience' in Herod's reaction: he feared John while alive and was troubled about him after death, though Herod himself never repented. He observes that 'seeds often spring up and bear fruit, when the sower, like John the Baptist, is dead or gone' — the prophet's influence outlasted his execution.

set: The chapter opens near Gennesaret in Jewish Galilee, then moves deliberately into Gentile territory — first Tyre, an old, wealthy Phoenician port city, then through Sidon and into the Decapolis.

his.t: Pharisees treated handed-down rules as nearly equal to the Law.
Tyre and Sidon were Phoenician cities with a mixed, mostly pagan population.

cus.t: Washing hands, cups and couches was a Pharisaic tradition, not a Mosaic command.
Calling goods "Corban" dedicated them to God, which some used to avoid helping parents.

cu: Ceremonial hand-washing before meals wasn't a hygiene practice but a ritual purity custom, extended by the Pharisees from priestly regulations to everyday eating. The "Corban" loophole let someone declare their assets "devoted to God," legally shielding wealth from supporting aging parents — a technically lawful maneuver Jesus calls out as nullifying God's actual command.

ot.n: The command to honor father and mother, quoted directly by Jesus against the Corban loophole.
"These people honor Me with their lips" — quoted directly by Jesus in v.6-7.
The Levitical dietary code, the backdrop against which the debate over v.19's meaning continues among readers today.

im.c: The Woman of Canaan at the Feet of Christ, by Jean-Germain Drouais (1784)

cm.n: Henry notes that hand-washing itself "was a cleanly custom, and no harm in it" — the real problem wasn't the practice but the Pharisees making it a binding religious law rather than a matter of personal choice.

On the Syrophoenician woman, Henry stresses just how far outside Israel's covenant she stood — "a stranger to the commonwealth of Israel, an alien to the covenant of promise," with no claim on Jesus by nationality or religion. Her persistence despite that, he suggests, is exactly what makes her faith so striking.

Ryle frames the central lesson plainly: 'the heart is the chief source of defilement and impurity in God's sight. Moral purity does not depend on washing or not washing — touching things or not touching them, eating things or not eating them, as the Scribes and Pharisees taught.' He commends anyone who, like the psalmist, prays 'teach me thy statutes' rather than resting…
